questions.stem:
A term infant is born by vaginal delivery to a mother whose HIV infection was diagnosed only at delivery and who received no antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy. Labor was prolonged, with membranes ruptured for 14 hours. The infant is formula fed. HIV nucleic acid testing of the infant is negative at 36 hours of life and positive at 6 weeks of age.

When was this infant most likely infected?
choices: In utero by transplacental passage before 36 weeks
During labor and delivery
Through breastfeeding after birth
Through postnatal contact with maternal saliva
From a transfusion during the newborn period

explain.html:
Without intervention, mother-to-infant transmission of HIV occurs in about 20 to 40% of exposed infants, across three risk periods. Antenatal (in utero) infection by transplacental passage, about 20% of perinatal cases in non-breastfeeding women and especially when the mother is infected during pregnancy, is detectable by PCR within the first 48 hours of life. Intrapartum infection, about 80% of cases, comes from exposure to maternal blood and vaginal secretions with placental separation, maternal-fetal microtransfusions, labor and rupture of membranes; the infant's PCR is negative at birth and becomes positive later. Breastfeeding from a viremic mother adds a postpartum window.

This infant's nucleic acid test was negative at 36 hours and positive at 6 weeks, he was formula fed, and his mother was untreated with membranes ruptured for 14 hours, a listed obstetric risk factor. The timing pattern places infection during labor and delivery, which is why most prevention targets the period around birth.
explain.table:
WindowShare of perinatal casesInfant PCR
In utero (antenatal)About 20%Positive within 48 hours of life
Intrapartum (labor and delivery)About 80%Negative at birth, positive later
Postpartum (breastfeeding)Additional 20 to 25% without maternal treatmentTurns positive after breast milk exposure
why: In utero infection would usually make the PCR positive within the first 48 hours, and his test at 36 hours was negative.
The infant is formula fed, so the breastfeeding window does not apply.
Contact with maternal saliva is not one of the three risk periods for perinatal transmission.
Nothing in the history describes a transfusion, and the timing pattern already fits intrapartum exposure.
explain.takeaway: About 80% of perinatal HIV transmission occurs during labor and delivery; in utero infection is PCR positive within 48 hours, whereas intrapartum infection is PCR negative at birth and positive later.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize timing of perinatal HIV transmission and and maternal risk factors for transmission

rows.if_right: a positive nucleic acid test within the first 48 hours of life

rows.why: The infant is formula fed, so the breastfeeding window does not apply.
rows.if_right: a breastfed infant of a viremic mother who turns positive after early negative tests

rows.why: Contact with maternal saliva is not one of the three risk periods for perinatal transmission.
rows.if_right: no scenario; saliva is not a listed route

rows.why: Nothing in the history describes a transfusion, and the timing pattern already fits intrapartum exposure.
rows.if_right: a documented transfusion of infected blood in the newborn period

questions.stem:
Four pregnant women with HIV infection are seen in a prenatal clinic at 34 weeks. All plan to formula feed.

[[labs 0]]

Which feature most strongly predicts the risk that Woman 3's infant will acquire HIV?
choices: Her CD4 count
Her plan to formula feed
Her plasma viral load
Her gestational age at this visit
Her choice of antiretroviral drugs later

explain.html:
The lecture divides risk factors for perinatal HIV transmission into two groups. Laboratory risk factors are a high maternal viral load and a low maternal CD4 count. Obstetric risk factors are rupture of membranes for more than 4 hours, chorioamnionitis and invasive monitoring such as scalp electrodes. Of all of these, maternal viral load is the major predictor of transmission.

That is why the central prevention goal is to identify women before conception, assure antiretroviral treatment, and keep every woman undetectable throughout pregnancy and at delivery. Woman 3 is untreated with a viral load of 210,000, so her plasma viral load is the feature that most strongly predicts her infant's risk; her low CD4 adds risk but is not the major predictor, and formula feeding lowers rather than raises it.
explain.table:
Risk factor groupExamples
LaboratoryHigh maternal viral load (major predictor); low maternal CD4
ObstetricRupture of membranes over 4 hours; chorioamnionitis; scalp electrodes
FeedingBreastfeeding by a viremic mother
why: A low maternal CD4 is a listed laboratory risk factor, but viral load is the major predictor.
Formula feeding eliminates the breastfeeding window and lowers risk rather than predicting it.
Gestational age at a clinic visit is not a listed risk factor for transmission.
Drug choice matters only through its effect on viral load, which is the true predictor.
explain.takeaway: Maternal viral load is the major predictor of perinatal HIV transmission, so the prevention goal is an undetectable viral load throughout pregnancy and at delivery.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize timing of perinatal HIV transmission and and maternal risk factors for transmission

rows.if_right: a mother with undetectable viral load, where low CD4 is the remaining listed risk factor

rows.if_right: a newborn born before 37 weeks on the perinatal risk screen

rows.if_right: a mother whose current regimen is failing to suppress her viral load

questions.stem:
A 5-month-old boy born to a mother with HIV is seen for a well visit. He has been formula fed since birth and completed newborn antiretroviral prophylaxis. His HIV nucleic acid tests were negative at 16 days, at 6 weeks, and again at 4 1/2 months. He is growing well, and his examination is normal.

Which of the following best describes his HIV status?
choices: Infection is excluded
Infection cannot be excluded until an antibody test at 18 months
Infection cannot be excluded until he has three more virologic tests
He should be treated presumptively with three-drug ART
He must have a CD4 percentage measured to determine status

explain.html:
Infants born to mothers with HIV get HIV nucleic acid testing at three time points: 14 to 21 days, 1 to 2 months and 4 to 6 months, with extra tests for higher-risk infants. In a non-breastfed infant, HIV is excluded by two or more negative virologic tests, with one at 1 month of age or older and one at 4 months or older. An alternative route is two or more negative antibody tests performed at 6 months or older, but that is not required when the virologic criteria are met. CD4 values describe immune status in a known infection, not whether infection is present.

This boy is formula fed and has negative NATs at 16 days, 6 weeks and 4 1/2 months. The 6-week test satisfies the 1-month requirement and the 4 1/2-month test satisfies the 4-month requirement, so infection is excluded.
explain.table:
TimingTestPurpose
BirthNAT (higher-risk infants)Detect in utero infection
14 to 21 daysNATRoutine
1 to 2 monthsNATCounts as the 1 month or older negative
4 to 6 monthsNATCounts as the 4 months or older negative
6 months or olderTwo or more antibody testsAlternative way to exclude infection
why: Antibody testing is an alternative after 6 months, not a requirement when virologic criteria are met, and 18 months is not the exclusion rule.
Two qualifying negative virologic tests are sufficient, and he already has them.
He has no evidence of infection, so three-drug ART is not indicated.
CD4 percentage stages a known infection and does not determine whether infection is present.
explain.takeaway: In a non-breastfed infant, HIV is excluded by two or more negative virologic tests, one at 1 month or older and one at 4 months or older.
explain.topic: Excluding infection in a non-breastfed infant
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Know how newborns born to HIV-infected persons are screened

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old woman with HIV infection is seen at 35 weeks of gestation. She started antiretroviral therapy late in pregnancy and has had trouble taking it consistently. Her plasma HIV RNA at 34 weeks is 8,400 copies/mL. She is not in labor, and her membranes are intact.

Which delivery plan best reduces the infant's risk of HIV acquisition?
choices: Induction of labor at 36 weeks with fetal scalp electrode monitoring
Planned vaginal delivery after spontaneous labor
Early artificial rupture of membranes to shorten labor
Vaginal delivery once her viral load is rechecked in labor
Scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks

explain.html:
Since about 80% of perinatal transmission takes place close to or during labor and delivery, prevention works on two fronts. The first is reducing maternal viral load, the major predictor of transmission, with ART and a goal of undetectable through delivery. The second is reducing exposure to HIV during delivery: an elective scheduled cesarean section at 38 weeks is recommended for women with HIV RNA above 1,000 copies/mL or an unknown level near the time of delivery. The listed obstetric risk factors, rupture of membranes for more than 4 hours, chorioamnionitis and invasive monitoring such as scalp electrodes, should be avoided.

This woman started ART late, adheres poorly and has a viral load of 8,400 at 34 weeks with intact membranes. She meets the threshold, so a scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks best reduces her infant's exposure.
why: Fetal scalp electrodes are invasive monitoring, a listed obstetric risk factor that raises transmission.
With a viral load above 1,000, vaginal delivery leaves the infant exposed to maternal blood and secretions in labor.
Early artificial rupture prolongs ruptured membranes, and rupture over 4 hours is a listed risk factor.
Her viral load near delivery is already above 1,000, which is the indication for cesarean, so waiting to recheck in labor loses the planned window.
explain.takeaway: Women with HIV RNA above 1,000 copies/mL or an unknown viral load near delivery should have a scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks to reduce intrapartum exposure.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize the interventions to prevent perinatal transmission

rows.why: Fetal scalp electrodes are invasive monitoring, a listed obstetric risk factor that raises transmission.
rows.if_right: no scenario; scalp electrodes are avoided in HIV

rows.why: With a viral load above 1,000, vaginal delivery leaves the infant exposed to maternal blood and secretions in labor.
rows.if_right: an undetectable viral load near delivery

rows.why: Early artificial rupture prolongs ruptured membranes, and rupture over 4 hours is a listed risk factor.
rows.if_right: no scenario; prolonged rupture is avoided

rows.why: Her viral load near delivery is already above 1,000, which is the indication for cesarean, so waiting to recheck in labor loses the planned window.

questions.stem:
A term boy (39 weeks) is born by vaginal delivery to a 30-year-old woman with HIV. She attended 12 prenatal visits, took ART throughout pregnancy with documented adherence, and had an undetectable viral load on every test, including at 37 weeks. She had no sexually transmitted infections, no prolonged rupture of membranes, and no chorioamnionitis. She plans to formula feed.

Which of the following is the most appropriate neonatal prophylaxis?
choices: Zidovudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine for 6 weeks
Zidovudine, lamivudine, and raltegravir for 2 weeks
No prophylaxis, because the mother is suppressed
Lamivudine alone for 6 weeks
Zidovudine alone for 2 weeks

explain.html:
After delivery, every HIV-exposed newborn receives post-exposure prophylaxis, and the intensity is set by the perinatal transmission risk screen. The screen asks whether the mother had adequate HIV care (viral load monitoring and testing at 36 weeks or later), adequate prenatal care of at least 10 visits, documented adherence with at least 10 weeks of ART, and sustained viral suppression; whether she had acute HIV, other infections or obstetric complications such as PROM or chorioamnionitis; whether she intends to breastfeed; and whether the newborn is 37 weeks or more. If every answer falls in the reassuring column, the exposure is low risk and the infant receives zidovudine alone for 2 weeks.

If any one answer falls in the other column, the exposure is moderate to high and the infant receives zidovudine for 4 to 6 weeks or a three-drug regimen. This mother had 12 visits, adherent ART throughout, undetectable loads including at 37 weeks, no complications and plans to formula feed a 39-week infant, so every item is reassuring.
explain.table:
Exposure riskWhenNeonatal prophylaxis
LowEvery screen item reassuringZidovudine for 2 weeks
Moderate to highAny one item not metZidovudine 4 to 6 weeks, or ZDV, 3TC and NVP or RAL for 2 to 6 weeks
why: A three-drug regimen for 6 weeks is reserved for moderate- to high-risk exposures.
Zidovudine, lamivudine and raltegravir is also a moderate- to high-risk regimen.
Even low-risk exposed newborns receive post-exposure prophylaxis.
Lamivudine alone is not a listed neonatal prophylaxis option.
explain.takeaway: Newborns with a low-risk perinatal exposure (suppressed, adherent mother with adequate care, term, formula fed) receive zidovudine alone for 2 weeks; any risk factor upgrades to longer or multidrug prophylaxis.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize the interventions to prevent perinatal transmission

rows.why: A three-drug regimen for 6 weeks is reserved for moderate- to high-risk exposures.
rows.if_right: a mother with a detectable viral load, missed care, breastfeeding plans or a preterm infant

rows.why: Zidovudine, lamivudine and raltegravir is also a moderate- to high-risk regimen.
rows.if_right: any one unfavorable item on the risk screen, such as chorioamnionitis

rows.why: Even low-risk exposed newborns receive post-exposure prophylaxis.
rows.if_right: no scenario; every exposed newborn receives prophylaxis

questions.stem:
A 4-year-old girl with perinatally acquired HIV infection comes for routine immunizations. She was diagnosed late and started antiretroviral therapy 2 months ago. Her CD4 count is 280/mm3 (11%), consistent with severe immunosuppression for her age. She is due for several vaccines.

Which vaccine should be withheld at this time?
choices: Inactivated influenza vaccine
Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine
Measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine
Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine
Meningococcal conjugate vaccine

explain.html:
Vaccination of children with HIV splits by vaccine type. All inactivated vaccines are safe irrespective of immune status and are given on the standard schedule, and children with HIV also need Pneumovax (pneumococcal polysaccharide) and Hib if not given in infancy, plus an early meningococcal series. Live vaccines depend on the degree of immunosuppression. MMR and varicella are recommended for children with low-level or no immunosuppression but not for those with high-level immunosuppression, live intranasal influenza is not recommended at all, and live rotavirus is recommended for all.

This 4-year-old's CD4 of 280 (11%) is below the 500 and 22% cutoffs for her age, which is stage 3, severe immunosuppression. Of the vaccines listed, MMR is the only live vaccine, so it is the one to withhold until her immune status improves on ART.
explain.table:
VaccineTypeChild with HIV
Inactivated influenza, Hib, pneumococcal, meningococcalInactivatedGive regardless of immune status
MMRLiveGive only with low-level or no immunosuppression
VaricellaLiveGive only with low-level or no immunosuppression
Live influenzaLiveNot recommended
RotavirusLiveRecommended for all
why: Inactivated influenza vaccine is safe at any CD4 level.
Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is inactivated and is an extra vaccine recommended in HIV.
Hib vaccine is inactivated and is recommended for children with HIV.
Meningococcal vaccine is inactivated, and the series should start early in HIV.
explain.takeaway: Children with HIV receive all inactivated vaccines regardless of immune status; live MMR and varicella are withheld with high-level immunosuppression, live influenza is not given, and rotavirus is given to all.
explain.topic: Live vaccines in children with HIV
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: What are signs and symptom of pediatric HIV infection

questions.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought for evaluation. Over the past year he has had six episodes of otitis media, two pneumonias, and oral thrush that returned despite standard antifungal treatment. He has fallen from the 50th to below the 5th percentile for weight. He says only a few words, and examination shows bilateral parotid enlargement, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and increased tone with brisk reflexes in both legs. His mother's HIV status was never documented.

His speech delay and leg findings are most consistent with which of the following?
choices: HIV encephalopathy
Cerebral toxoplasmosis
Cryptococcal meningitis
A cerebellar tumor
Bacterial meningitis sequelae

explain.html:
The high-yield signs of pediatric HIV include unusually frequent and severe common bacterial infections (otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia), recurrent thrush that does not respond to standard antifungals (suggesting lymphocyte dysfunction), growth failure and failure to thrive, and opportunistic infections. On examination, parotid enlargement, generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are concerning findings. Failure to attain milestones, particularly impaired expressive language, may indicate HIV encephalopathy, and spastic diplegia that looks like cerebral palsy can develop.

This 2-year-old has recurrent otitis and pneumonia, refractory thrush, falling weight, parotid enlargement, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, with an undocumented maternal status. His few words and increased tone with brisk reflexes in both legs are the developmental delay and spastic diplegia of HIV encephalopathy, as in the lecture's toddler with hyperreflexia and clonus who improved as the virus was suppressed.
why: Pediatric HIV toxoplasmosis counts only with onset before 1 month of age, and nothing here suggests focal lesions.
Cryptococcal meningitis is not a pediatric HIV presentation here and would not explain developmental delay with diplegia.
Nothing points to a posterior fossa mass, and the findings are spastic rather than cerebellar.
No history of meningitis is given, and a single bacterial meningitis is a separate category from encephalopathy.
explain.takeaway: Pediatric HIV presents with recurrent bacterial infections, refractory thrush, failure to thrive, parotid enlargement and organomegaly; developmental delay with expressive language impairment and spastic diplegia suggest HIV encephalopathy.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: What are signs and symptom of pediatric HIV infection

rows.if_right: an infant with toxoplasmosis beginning before 1 month of age

rows.why: Cryptococcal meningitis is not a pediatric HIV presentation here and would not explain developmental delay with diplegia.
rows.if_right: an adult with CD4 below 100, headache and a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen

rows.why: Nothing points to a posterior fossa mass, and the findings are spastic rather than cerebellar.
rows.if_right: a child with ataxia and a posterior fossa mass on imaging

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old woman with HIV has taken antiretroviral therapy since before conception and has had an undetectable viral load throughout pregnancy. She delivers a healthy term infant. She tells the team that breastfeeding is important to her family and asks what the current U.S. recommendation is.

Which of the following best reflects current guidance?
choices: Breastfeeding is prohibited for all people with HIV
Breastfeeding carries no risk when the viral load is undetectable
Shared decision-making, noting risk below 1% but not zero
Breastfeed only after the infant's 6-month antibody test is negative
Breastfeeding is allowed only if the infant takes no prophylaxis

explain.html:
From 1990 to 2023 the US standard was a strong recommendation to avoid breastfeeding, unlike many low- and middle-income countries where formula cost and unsafe water raise infant mortality. Guidance updated on January 31, 2023 now calls for evidence-based, patient-centered counseling that supports shared decision-making about infant feeding, starting before conception or as early as possible in pregnancy and revisited after delivery. The team then helps implement the family's plan. Formula feeding eliminates transmission risk. With viral suppression maintained on ART during pregnancy and postpartum, breastfeeding transmission falls to below 1%, but not zero, estimated at 0.3% at 6 months and 0.6% at 12 months of exclusive breastfeeding.

This mother has been on ART since before conception with an undetectable viral load throughout pregnancy, and breastfeeding matters to her family. The current answer is shared decision-making with honest counseling about that small residual risk.
explain.table:
Feeding planTransmission risk
Formula feedingEliminated
Breastfeeding with sustained maternal suppressionBelow 1%, not zero (0.3% at 6 months, 0.6% at 12 months)
Breastfeeding without maternal treatmentAdditional 20 to 25% of infants infected
why: Avoidance was the old 1990 to 2023 standard; current guidance supports shared decision-making.
With suppression the risk falls below 1% but is not zero.
Antibody tests are unreliable in infants, and feeding decisions cannot wait 6 months.
Infant prophylaxis is still given and is not a condition that blocks breastfeeding.
explain.takeaway: Current US guidance (2023) supports shared decision-making on infant feeding: formula eliminates risk, while breastfeeding with sustained maternal suppression carries a risk below 1% but not zero.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize options for infant feeding among HIV infected persons

questions.stem:
A 3-month-old girl is seen for follow-up. Her mother has HIV infection, was virally suppressed throughout pregnancy, and formula feeds. The infant received zidovudine for 2 weeks after birth and is thriving. A rapid HIV antibody test performed on the infant in the emergency department during a minor illness is reactive. HIV nucleic acid tests at 18 days and at 6 weeks were both negative.

Which of the following best explains the reactive antibody test?
choices: She has acute HIV infection
Maternal IgG crossed the placenta
She made antibodies after zidovudine exposure
Breast milk antibodies were absorbed
Infant IgM against HIV is being produced

explain.html:
HIV-exposed infants cannot be diagnosed with antibody tests early in life, because maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and every exposed infant tests antibody positive whether or not infected. For this reason a virologic assay (HIV nucleic acid testing, NAT) that directly detects HIV RNA or DNA is required to diagnose HIV in perinatally exposed infants younger than 18 months. The recommended schedule is NAT at 14 to 21 days, 1 to 2 months and 4 to 6 months, with added tests at birth and 2 to 6 weeks after stopping prophylaxis for higher-risk infants. Antibody testing becomes useful only later, when two or more negative antibody tests at 6 months or older can exclude infection.

This 3-month-old's mother was suppressed, she is formula fed and thriving, and her NATs at 18 days and 6 weeks were negative. The reactive rapid antibody test therefore reflects her mother's IgG, not infection.
why: Two negative virologic tests make infection unlikely, and an antibody test cannot diagnose infection at this age.
Antiretroviral drugs such as zidovudine do not provoke HIV antibodies.
She is formula fed, so breast milk is not a source, and placental IgG explains the result.
An infant making HIV-specific antibody would imply infection, which her negative NATs argue against.
explain.takeaway: Maternal IgG makes HIV-exposed infants antibody positive for months, so infants under 18 months are diagnosed with virologic nucleic acid tests, not antibody tests.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Know how newborns born to HIV-infected persons are screened

rows.if_right: a positive HIV nucleic acid test rather than an antibody test

rows.why: Antiretroviral drugs such as zidovudine do not provoke HIV antibodies.
rows.if_right: no scenario; prophylaxis does not cause a reactive antibody test

rows.if_right: no scenario in a formula-fed infant

rows.why: An infant making HIV-specific antibody would imply infection, which her negative NATs argue against.
rows.if_right: positive virologic tests confirming infection

questions.stem:
A 20-year-old woman with no prenatal care arrives in active labor at 39 weeks. Her HIV status is unknown, and an expedited HIV test is reactive. Supplemental confirmatory testing will take more than a day. She had planned to breastfeed. She delivers a healthy term girl by cesarean.

Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for the newborn?
choices: Await confirmatory maternal testing before giving the infant any medication
Start zidovudine alone for 2 weeks and allow breastfeeding
Test the infant for HIV antibody at 18 months before deciding
Start three-drug ART within 6 hours and hold breastfeeding
Give a single dose of nevirapine and test the infant at 6 months

explain.html:
A positive HIV screen during labor and delivery requires immediate attention and supplemental maternal testing as soon as possible, and until conclusive results are available the patient is presumed positive. The team then starts the perinatal HIV prevention care cascade. For the mother: oral ART and intravenous zidovudine (a loading dose then continuous infusion). For feeding: hold breastfeeding. For the infant, who is considered a high-risk exposure: three-drug ART within 6 hours of delivery (zidovudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine or raltegravir), and virologic testing (HIV RNA or DNA NAT) at birth.

This mother had no prenatal care, has a reactive expedited test with confirmation more than a day away and wanted to breastfeed. Waiting would lose the protective window, so the newborn starts three-drug ART within 6 hours while breastfeeding is held; single-drug zidovudine is reserved for low-risk exposures.

StepAction
1Maternal oral ART
2Maternal IV zidovudine
3Hold breastfeeding
4Infant three-drug ART within 6 hours (ZDV, 3TC, NVP or RAL)
5Infant virologic testing (NAT) at birth
why: Waiting for confirmation loses the protective window; the mother is presumed positive until proven otherwise.
Zidovudine alone is for low-risk exposures, and breastfeeding should be held here.
Antibody tests cannot diagnose exposed infants under 18 months, and decisions are needed now.
A single nevirapine dose is not the regimen the cascade lists, and testing must begin at birth, not 6 months.
explain.takeaway: With a preliminary positive HIV screen in labor, presume infection: maternal ART and IV zidovudine, hold breastfeeding, infant three-drug ART within 6 hours, and infant NAT at birth.

explain.objective: Recognize the interventions to prevent perinatal transmission

questions.stem:
An 11-month-old boy with perinatally acquired HIV infection is evaluated after recurrent ear infections and thrush that responded poorly to standard treatment. His CD4 results are below. A parent notes that the count "looks normal for an adult."

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following best describes his immune status?
choices: Normal, because the absolute count is above 500/mm3
Mild suppression, because the absolute count is near the adult range
Unable to judge until he turns 6 years old
Severe suppression, judged by age-specific cutoffs
Mild suppression, because the CD4 percentage is above 14%

explain.html:
CD4 levels vary with age: the absolute CD4 count is high in children under 6 years, so adult cutoffs do not apply. The CD4 percentage varies less than the count, which is why it is often used in pediatric HIV management, and staging uses age-specific values for under 1 year, 1 to under 6 years, and 6 years and older. For an infant under 1 year, stage 3 is a count below 750 or a percentage below 26%.

This 11-month-old's count of 700 would be normal for an adult, and his 20% would be stage 2 for a child 6 or older, but by the infant cutoffs both values are stage 3, severe immunosuppression. That matches his recurrent ear infections and thrush that responded poorly to treatment, both high-yield signs of pediatric HIV.

StageUnder 1 year1 to under 6 years6 years and older
11,500 or more; 34% or more1,000 or more; 30% or more500 or more; 26% or more
2750 to 1,499; 26 to 33%500 to 999; 22 to 29%200 to 499; 14 to 25%
3Under 750; under 26%Under 500; under 22%Under 200; under 14%
why: Adult cutoffs do not apply because young children normally have much higher absolute counts.
Infant cutoffs are much higher than adult ones, and both of his values fall in the severe range.
Age-specific staging exists for children under 6, so his status can be judged now.
The 14% cutoff applies to children 6 and older; under 1 year, below 26% is severe.
explain.takeaway: Young children have higher absolute CD4 counts, so pediatric HIV is staged with age-specific values and often by CD4 percentage; under 1 year, below 750 or below 26% is stage 3.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Be able to interpret CD4 counts in children of various ages and levels of immunosuppression

questions.stem:
A 6-month-old girl is seen for follow-up. Her mother has HIV infection, took antiretroviral therapy throughout pregnancy, and had an undetectable viral load at delivery. After shared decision-making, she chose to breastfeed and still exclusively breastfeeds. The infant completed newborn zidovudine prophylaxis. Infant HIV nucleic acid tests at 18 days, 6 weeks, and 4 months were all negative. At a visit last month the mother admitted she stopped her own ART when the infant was 3 months old, and her viral load is now 38,000 copies/mL. The infant is thriving with a normal examination.

Which statement best describes the infant's HIV status?
choices: Excluded, since she had negative virologic tests at 1 and 4 months
Excluded, since most perinatal infection occurs around delivery
Not excluded, since breastfeeding from a viremic mother continues
Infected, since a viremic mother who breastfeeds nearly always transmits
Unknown until an antibody test at 18 months, since NAT is unreliable

explain.html:
Perinatal HIV transmission happens in three windows: in utero, peripartum, and postpartum through breastfeeding, which adds about 20% to 25% risk when the mother is viremic and untreated. With maternal suppression on ART, breastfeeding risk falls below 1%, but that protection lasts only as long as the suppression. Because maternal viral load is the major predictor, a mother who stops ART while breastfeeding re-exposes her infant.

Infants under 18 months are diagnosed with virologic tests (HIV RNA or DNA), since antibody may be maternal. Infection can be excluded in a non-breastfed infant with two negative virologic tests, one at 1 month or older and one at 4 months or older. This infant meets that pattern on paper, but she is still breastfeeding from a mother with 38,000 copies/mL, so her exposure has not ended and her status cannot be called excluded; testing continues during and after breastfeeding.
explain.table:
SituationCan two negative virologic tests (1 and 4 months) exclude infection?
Formula fed, exposure ended at birthYes
Breastfed, mother suppressed on ARTNot while exposure continues; risk below 1% but not zero
Breastfed, mother viremicNo; ongoing exposure with substantial risk
why: The two-negative-test rule is written for non-breastfed infants, and this infant is still exposed through breast milk.
Peripartum transmission is the largest share, but breastfeeding from a viremic mother adds real postnatal risk.
Breastfeeding adds about 20% to 25% risk without maternal treatment, a large risk but far from certain transmission.
Virologic tests are required under 18 months, and an antibody result in infancy reflects maternal IgG.
explain.takeaway: Negative infant virologic tests exclude HIV only after exposure ends; breastfeeding from a viremic mother is ongoing exposure, so testing continues through and after weaning.
explain.topic: Ongoing breastfeeding exposure and excluding infant infection

explain.objective: Know how newborns born to HIV-infected persons are screened

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman had a negative HIV test at her first prenatal visit at 9 weeks of gestation. At about 20 weeks, soon after starting a relationship with a new partner, she had a week of fever, sore throat, and rash but did not seek care, and she missed her later visits. She arrived in labor at 39 weeks; an expedited HIV test was reactive, with a viral load of 640,000 copies/mL. Membranes had been ruptured for 9 hours before a vaginal delivery. The infant was started on three-drug ART within 6 hours and is formula fed. HIV nucleic acid testing of the infant at 30 hours of life is positive.

Which measure would most likely have prevented this infant's infection?
choices: Avoiding membrane rupture longer than 4 hours
Starting the infant's three-drug ART at birth
Giving the mother IV zidovudine during labor
HIV testing at her febrile illness, then ART
A scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks

explain.html:
Perinatal HIV transmission has distinct timing windows. About 20% of non-breastfed cases occur in utero, before 36 weeks, and these infants have a positive virologic test within the first 48 hours of life; in utero transmission is especially likely if the mother becomes infected during pregnancy. About 80% occur peripartum, close to or during labor and delivery, and those infants test negative at birth and positive later. Risk factors include high maternal viral load and low CD4 count, and obstetric factors such as membrane rupture longer than 4 hours, chorioamnionitis and scalp electrodes.

Prevention works only inside the right window. Pregnant women are tested early, again in the third trimester, and whenever there are signs and symptoms of acute HIV, so ART can drive the viral load down, the major predictor of transmission. This mother's fever, sore throat and rash after a new partner at 20 weeks was acute HIV, and her infant's positive test at 30 hours places infection in utero. Testing and treating her then is the only listed measure that acts before the infection occurred.
explain.table:
TimingShare of casesInfant virologic testMeasures that act in this window
In utero (before 36 weeks)About 20%Positive within 48 hoursMaternal testing and ART during pregnancy
PeripartumAbout 80%Negative at birth, positive laterCesarean for high viral load, IV zidovudine, neonatal prophylaxis
BreastfeedingAdded risk if mother viremicNegative early, positive laterMaternal suppression or formula
why: Membrane rupture over 4 hours is an intrapartum risk factor, and this infection predates labor.
Neonatal ART is post-exposure prophylaxis; it cannot reverse an infection that was established in utero.
Intravenous zidovudine in labor protects against intrapartum transmission, which comes after the in utero infection seen here.
Cesarean prevents exposure to blood and secretions during delivery, but this infant was already infected before labor began.
explain.takeaway: A positive infant HIV nucleic acid test within 48 hours means in utero infection, most often after maternal infection during pregnancy; preventing it requires antepartum diagnosis and maternal ART.
explain.topic: In utero transmission and the missed window for prevention
